power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .692", "p = .204", "p = .059", "p = .174" ), Sentence = c("For task performance, the inclusion of quadratic terms in Model 2 did not significantly improve model fit (Δ adjusted R² = -.004, p = .692).", "For contextual performance, the addition of quadratic terms in Model 2 again did not significantly improve model fit (Δ adjusted R² = .004, p = .204).", "For adaptive performance, neither the linear model (adjusted R² = .011, p = .059) nor the addition of quadratic terms (Δ adjusted R² = .005, p = .174) yielded meaningful effects, and no individual predictors reached significance.", "For adaptive performance, neither the linear model (adjusted R² = .011, p = .059) nor the addition of quadratic terms (Δ adjusted R² = .005, p = .174) yielded meaningful effects, and no individual predictors reached significance." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. info.title: Mapping and Understanding Employees' Perceived Personality-Work (Mis)Fit: a Mixed-Method Approach

text.text: Although perceived person-environment (P-E) fit has been extensively studied and linked to important workplace outcomes, it has not been examined with the same level of attribute specificity as objective fit.
This study addressed that gap by introducing and empirically examining perceived personality-work (mis)fit.

Employing a multi-method, multi-informant design with 734 employees and 521 supervisors, we aimed to ( a)operationalize perceived personality-work (mis)fit using the too little/too much scale, (b) explore the workplace experiences that shape these perceptions, and (c) examine how they relate to supervisor-rated job performance.

text.text: We found a high prevalence of perceived misfit, with both deficiency (30%) and excess (42%) commonly reported, while perceived fit was observed across a range of personality trait levels.

Thematic analysis revealed that negative experiences associated with perceived misfit extended beyond task performance, encompassing well-being concerns and interpersonal difficulties, with distinct patterns across traits.
Finally, perceived personality-work (mis)fit showed modest associations with supervisor-rated job performance.

Theoretically, these findings provide insight into how employees experience the fit of their personality at work and highlight the value of examining perceived fit with respect to specific personal attributes.
Practically, they inform efforts to better support employees' fit experiences in the workplace.
Employees' attitudes and behaviours are shaped not only by the realities of their work environment but also by how they perceive their fit within it.

This subjective perception is captured by the concept of perceived person-environment (P-E) fit, which refers to individuals' own judgments about how well they fit a particular job or organization at a given point in time (De Cooman & Vleugels, 2022; Su et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This subjective perception is captured by the concept of perceived <ref type="bibr">person-environment (P-E)</ref> fit, which refers to individuals' own judgments about how well they fit a particular job or organization at a given point in time <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(De Cooman & Vleugels, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Su et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike objective fit, which is inferred from explicit comparisons between personal and environmental attributes, perceived fit is grounded in employees' own interpretations of compatibility.

Meta-analytic evidence has consistently shown that perceived fit is associated with a wide range of work-related outcomes, including job satisfaction, organizational commitment, and job performance (Arthur et al., 2006; Kristof-Brown et al., 2005).

text.text: Moreover, perceived fit often demonstrates stronger relationships with some of these outcomes than objective fit, leading scholars to argue that it is a more proximal determinant of employees' attitudes and decisions ( Kristof-Brown & Billsberry, 2013).

text.text: However, research on perceived fit remains limited by its lack of attribute-level specificity.

Objective fit research has extensively examined how particular employee characteristics-such as needs, goals, abilities, personality traits, and values-align with features of the work environment (De Cooman & Vleugels, 2022).

text.text: In contrast, perceived fit is typically conceptualized and measured as a holistic psychological experience reflecting an overall sense of compatibility with one's job or organization (Englert et al., 2023; Su et al., 2015; van Vianen, 2018).

text.text: Consequently, little is known about how employees perceive the fit of specific personal attributes.
Personality constitutes a particularly relevant attribute given its established links to important work outcomes (Wilmot et al., 2019; Wilmot & Ones, 2019).

text.text: Studies of objective personality-environment fit typically compare employees' self-reported traits with externally derived estimates of occupational or job trait requirements (e.g., Ghetta et al., 2020; Juchem et al., 2026).

text.text: Although this approach has generated valuable insights into personality fit and outcomes such as job satisfaction and career development, it reveals little about employees' own perceptions of personality-work fit.
The few studies that do address personality within perceived fit research tend to assess it at a broad, undifferentiated level.

For example, respondents may be asked to evaluate the overall match between their personality and the personality characteristics required by the job (Chuang et al., 2016) or to indicate their agreement with statements regarding the fit of their personality within a group (e.g., "I bring unique personality traits to this group"; Li et al., 2019).

text.text: As a result, little is known about how employees perceive the fit of specific personality traits or whether they experience misfit as a trait deficiency or excess.

To address this gap, we introduce the concept of "perceived personality-work (mis)fit", defined as the extent to which employees perceive that each of their personality traits aligns with the demands of their work, taking into account the direction (i.e., excess or deficiency) of any misfit.
The present study pursues three objectives.

First, we operationalize perceived personality-work (mis)fit using the Too Little/Too Much (TLTM) rating scale (Kaiser & Kaplan, 2005), a response format originally developed for leadership assessment.

text.text: This approach enables employees to indicate whether each personality trait is perceived as "too little," "too much," or "just right" for their work.

Second, we explore the factors underlying these perceptions using qualitative methods, responding to long-standing calls for greater insight into how fit perceptions are formed (Edwards et al., 2006; Su et al., 2015; van Vianen, 2018; Vleugels et al., 2018).

text.text: Third, building on the central premise of P-E fit theory that better fit is associated with more favourable outcomes (e.g., De Cooman & Vleugels, 2022), we examine the relationship between perceived personality-work (mis)fit and supervisor-rated job performance.

text.text: We propose two core criteria for effectively operationalizing perceived personalitywork (mis)fit: assessments should be trait-specific and should capture the direction of perceived misfit.

text.text: Specifically, employees may perceive fit with some traits while simultaneously experiencing misfit with others, and they may perceive such misfit as reflecting either too little or too much of a given trait relative to work demands.
The latter distinction parallels van Vianen's (2018) conceptualization of deficiency and excess as two forms of misfit.

In their review of broad P-E fit theory, these concepts are primarily defined from a needs-supplies perspective, whereby deficiency reflects a lack of valued attributes in the environment and excess reflects the presence of undesirable attributes (e.g., Kristof-Brown et al., 2005; van Vianen, 2018).

text.text: Because our focus is on personality traits and their alignment with job demands, we interpret these concepts from a demands-abilities perspective: deficiency refers to a perceived lack of a trait relative to work demands, whereas excess describes the perception of possessing more of a trait than is functional or desirable.

Given that adaptive traits such as conscientiousness and emotional stability are wellestablished predictors of positive work outcomes (e.g., Judge et al., 2002; Wilmot & Ones, 2019), it is reasonable to expect that employees may perceive deficiencies in these traits.

text.text: While their research focused on broader P-E fit and its fluctuations over time, the findings highlight the potential role of work experiences as meaningful cues.
One category of work experiences that may give rise to perceived personality-work misfit is performance-related challenges.

Because conscientiousness, extraversion, and emotional stability are positively associated with job performance (Wilmot & Ones, 2019; Zell & Lesick, 2022), employees who fail to meet performance expectations may perceive a deficiency in a trait they consider relevant to their role.

Perceived personality-work misfit may also stem from experiences beyond performance, including impaired well-being, job dissatisfaction, and interpersonal difficulties.
For instance, a large-scale review found that extraversion is associated not only with better performance but also with interpersonal, motivational, and emotional benefits (Wilmot et al., 2019).

For example, the perception of excess conscientiousness may originate from experiences of elevated stress and reduced well-being associated with higher levels of this trait (Carter et al., 2016).

text.text: Together, these examples suggest that a range of negative work experiences may contribute to perceived personality-work misfit.
The current study therefore seeks to identify and categorize these experiences:
Research Question 3 (RQ3): What types of negative work experiences do employees identify as origins of their perceived personality-work misfit?
To address this question, we use open-ended qualitative methods, which are wellsuited to uncovering how individuals make sense of their experiences (Willig, 2019).

text.text: By allowing employees to describe work experiences in their own words, this approach reveals the experiences they find most salient in shaping perceptions of misfit, while reducing the constraints and potential demand effects associated with structured inventories (Reja et al., 2003).

text.text: Importantly, employees may recognize that a single personality trait can support success in some areas while creating difficulties in others.

An open, exploratory approach thus enables a deeper understanding of which work experiences employees consider most important in shaping their perceived personality-work misfit (Vleugels et al., 2018).

text.text: Beyond understanding the origins of perceived personality-work (mis)fit, an important question is whether these perceptions relate to observable work outcomes-specifically, job performance as evaluated by supervisors.

Although perceived fit is generally associated with better performance (e.g., Kristof-Brown et al., 2005), it remains unclear whether this also applies to perceived personality-work (mis)fit, a more focused operationalization of fit relating to a single personal attribute.
text.formatted: Although perceived fit is generally associated with better performance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kristof-Brown et al., 2005)</ref>, it remains unclear whether this also applies to perceived personality-work (mis)fit, a more focused operationalization of fit relating to a single personal attribute.

text.text: Moreover, the effects of misfit may differ across its two forms: deficiency and excess.

Van Vianen's (2018) review on various forms of P-E fit suggests that both deficiency and excess can lead to negative outcomes, though deficiency-defined in that context as the environment falling short of personal preferences or valuesoften had stronger adverse effects.
Whether deficiency and excess have similar consequences can be examined by considering the shape of the relationship between perceived personality-work (mis)fit and job performance.
A curvilinear, inverted U-shaped relationship would suggest that both perceived deficiency and excess are associated with lower performance.
For example, among sales employees, perceiving either too little or too much extraversion for the role may be associated with performance decrements observable to supervisors (Grant, 2013).

For instance, perceiving too little emotional stability may impair employees' ability to cope with stress (Judge & Bono, 2001), whereas perceived excess may result in subtler interpersonal difficulties that are less likely to be reflected in performance evaluations.

text.text: Accordingly, the final aim of this study is to examine whether-and in what form (i.e., linear or curvilinear)-perceived personality-work (mis)fit across the Big Five traits is related to informant-rated job performance.

To capture a more nuanced understanding of job performance, we differentiate between three domains commonly identified in the literature: task, adaptive, and contextual performance (Pulakos et al., 2000; Renn & Fedor, 2001; Van Scotter and Motowidlo, 1996).

Method Participants and procedure A cross-sectional, multi-informant study design was used, combining quantitative and qualitative data collection.

For this purpose, undergraduate Belgian psychology students at Ghent University were asked to recruit one or more working adults to participate in this study as part of their course assignments or theses, yielding a sample of 734 participants who reported on the variables of interest.
Participating employees (62% women) had an average age of 43.89 years (SD = 11.62 years), with 75% holding a bachelor's degree or higher.

The sample represented various industries, with the largest proportions of participants employed in healthcare and welfare (19%), education (15%), manufacturing (9%), IT & communications (7%), and retail and wholesale (7%).

text.text: After completing the survey, participants were asked to invite their respective supervisors to provide observer ratings of their job performance.
Both employees and supervisors provided digital informed consent prior to participation and were explicitly assured that their responses would not be disclosed to the other party.
In total, 521 supervisors provided informant ratings.
Supervisors generally reported having frequent interactions with their employees, with only 10% indicating verbal interactions occurring less than once a week.
Moreover, 93% stated that they had worked with their employee for at least six months.

Employees' perceived personality-work (mis)fit was assessed using a Dutch adaptation of the validated Organizational Frame-of-reference Big-Five Personality Measure (ORG-B5; Pathki et al., 2022), which consists of 20 items (four items per Big Five dimension).

text.text: This personality inventory was selected due to its work frame of reference and brevity, which made it suitable for dual use: to evaluate perceived (mis)fit using the TLTM rating format, and to assess personality trait levels via the traditional Likert rating format (see below).

Following a back-translation of the original ORG-B5 into Dutch, each item was evaluated against two criteria to ensure its suitability for inclusion in the TLTM scale (see Dupré et al., 2022; Vergauwe et al., 2017).

text.text: These criteria involved (a) ensuring positive phrasing (i.e., avoiding reverse-scored items), and (b) removing evaluative elements in the items, given the scale's inherently evaluative nature.
As a result, nine out of twenty items required adaptation.
Some changes were relatively minor, such as rephrasing "I talk a lot at work" (extraversion) to "I am talkative at work".
Other items required more substantial revision because they contained words with strong evaluative connotations.
For example, "I am not easily bothered by things at work" (emotional stability), was changed into "I quickly move past difficult workplace situations" to avoid using the word "bothered".
Example items for the remaining domains are "I am prepared at work" (conscientiousness), "I care about others at work" (agreeableness), and "At work, I enjoy thinking about things" (openness).
A side-by-side overview of all items adapted for use with the TLTM scale is provided in the Supplementary Material.
Participants rated these items using a 5-point TLTM scale ranging from -2 (much too little) to 0 (the right amount) and +2 (much too much).

As shown in Table S1 in the Supplementary Material, Cronbach's alpha was acceptable for TLTM ratings of agreeableness (α = .76), extraversion (α = .76), conscientiousness (α = .78), and emotional stability (α = .60), but comparatively lower for openness (α = .41).

This question was: "For these last five statements we are additionally interested in the underlying rationale behind your answer.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four questionnaire versions, each containing open-ended questions for only one-quarter of the perceived (mis)fit items, thereby reducing fatigue and supporting response quality.
Although this open-ended question was non-obligatory, it generated a substantial pool of 1,225 responses, which were provided by 83% of the participants.
Job performance.
Supervisors provided informant ratings of employees' job performance using 11 items drawn from previous research (see Vergauwe et al., 2017).

text.text: These items encompassed three distinct performance areas: task performance, adaptive performance, and contextual performance (Pulakos et al., 2000; Renn & Fedor, 2001; Van Scotter & Motowidlo, 1996).

text.text: Example items are: "sets high-quality standards for work performance" (task performance), "maintains emotional control in crisis situations" (adaptive performance), and "helps someone without being asked" (contextual performance).

These items (see Supplementary Material) were presented alternating between performance domains, and supervisors were asked to rate them on a Likert scale ranging from "totally disagree" (1) to "totally agree" (5).

text.text: Internal consistencies were satisfactory for all three performance domains: task performance (α = .77), contextual performance (α = .76), and adaptive performance (α = .77).

The first author evaluated each response using eight categories to determine whether it was eligible for analysis (see Supplementary Material Table S6 for sample responses).

text.text: Overall, 70% of responses were deemed usable, of which 65% referenced negative work experiences and 5% included both negative and positive work experiences.
The remaining 30% were excluded because they did not describe negative work experiences.

Specifically, 8% paraphrased the perceived (mis)fit item or offered further clarification, and another 8% provided circumstantial justifications (i.e., situational reasons for behaviour rather than underlying perceived trait deficiencies or excesses).

In addition, 5% referred only to positive work experiences, 5% stated the absence of negative work experiences or simply wrote "/", and 4% were coded as "undecided" due to vagueness or inconsistency with the participant's selected perceived (mis)fit rating.

Next, we employed a hybrid thematic analysis (Proudfoot, 2023), combining predefined categories based on a theoretical framework (deductive coding), with themes generated from the data (inductive coding).

text.text: A preliminary set of eight categories was established based on an investigation of the literature on personality traits and their impact on work-related outcomes.

For example, we synthesized outcomes such as task performance (e.g., Hurtz & Donovan, 2000), innovative work behaviour (e.g., Woods et al., 2018), and leadership effectiveness (e.g., Derue et al., 2011) into a single category titled "Task performance and time management".

text.text: The primary author reviewed the first 20 responses for each Big Five domain using these predefined categories and subsequently assessed whether any modifications to the coding scheme were needed, including creating, merging, or renaming categories.
This systematic approach resulted in a final set of six distinct categories.
Responses were coded as Task performance and time management when they described declined task performance, a diminished ability to achieve results, and/or difficulties in managing time.
Adaptive performance was used for responses that described challenges in effectively adjusting to changing circumstances.
The Career and development opportunities category included responses that mentioned missed opportunities in terms of personal and/or career development.
Reputation at work encompassed responses that indicated leaving a negative impression on others at work.
Employees perceived that their coworkers held an unfavourable opinion about them, while not necessarily experiencing negative work experiences on a personal level.

Responses coded as Interpersonal difficulties at work described challenges in interacting with colleagues, clients, or superiors, which may encompass interactions both within and outside the work environment.
These challenges can range from difficulties in building friendships and conflicts with others to feelings of mistreatment and irritations with others.

The Well-being category compiled responses that included both mental difficulties (e.g., stress, decreased job satisfaction) and physical problems (e.g., sleep disturbances, headaches) within or outside the work environment.
It also encompasses issues in the personal sphere (e.g., limited work-life balance, interpersonal problems with friends).
An additional category, More information needed, was reserved for responses that lacked sufficient detail for categorization (e.g., "problems remain unsolved").

text.text: All responses were independently coded by the first author and a trained second rater (i.e., one of three master's students).
Raters were instructed to select two (or three) categories when respondents unambiguously mentioned multiple categories.
When considering only the first coded category, inter-rater agreement was substantial (86%; κ = .80).
The second coded category demonstrated a lower agreement percentage (51%), with 92% of disagreements arising because one rater identified a second category whereas the other did not.
All coding disagreements were resolved through a discussion between the first and second rater.
These discussions resulted in a final consensus for the coding of each response.

text.text: Note that domain-level results for openness, and to a lesser extent conscientiousness, should be interpreted cautiously, as item-level ratings may not consistently exhibit the necessary covariation for seamless aggregation to the domain level.
Across the Big Five traits, 30.4% of ratings reflected perceived fit, 41.9% reflected excess, and 27.6% reflected deficiency.
When examining individual Big Five traits, both deficiency and excess were endorsed for each of the traits.
Notably, the response pattern for emotional stability differed from that of the other Big Five traits, with a majority of employees (61.3%) perceiving their emotional stability at work as deficient.
In contrast, perceived deficiency for the other traits ranged from 11.2% to 28.6%.
We then examined interrelations between perceived TLTM-rated personality-work (mis)fit and Likert-rated personality trait levels at the domain level.
This provides insight into which Likert ratings on the five-point scale are typically associated with perceptions of deficiency, excess, or fit.

Findings in Table S1 (Supplementary Material) first show high positive correlations between corresponding domains, ranging between r = .54 (agreeableness and openness) and r = .68 (emotional stability), indicating that higher personality trait levels were associated with TLTM ratings leaning towards "excess" (too much), whereas lower personality trait levels were associated with ratings leaning towards "deficiency" (too little).

text.text: For clarity, "much too little" and "too little" were combined, as were "much too much" and "too much."
Percentages for personality trait level 1 should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of respondents in this category.
Findings reveal that personality trait levels of 1 and 2 predominantly corresponded to perceptions of deficiency (72% and 73%, respectively).
Respondents who rated their personality traits as a 3 or 4 primarily regarded them as "the right amount" (68% and 69%, respectively).

Lastly, for the maximum personality trait level (5), the majority of employees perceived their traits as "the right amount" (52%) for their work, while a significant portion of participants reported an excess in that trait (46%).
Notably, these distributions demonstrate that "the right amount" (fit) can correspond to personality trait levels ranging from 1 to 5.
These patterns were also generally consistent across personality domains.
The origins of employees' perceived personality-work misfit were examined in three ways.
First, we assessed the prevalence of negative work experience categories across domains, regardless of misfit direction.
Second, we examined these trends within each Big Five domain to identify potential differences in the categories most frequently mentioned across domains.
Third, we differentiated between open responses that preceded a perceived personality-work misfit rating of "too little" (deficiency) versus "too much" (excess).

Employees' descriptions of negative work experiences predominantly related to wellbeing (39%), task performance and time management (24%), interpersonal difficulties at work (22%), and reputation at work (6%).
Notably, only 1% of responses fell within the adaptive performance category, while responses related to career and development opportunities were extremely rare (only 4 mentions).
The remaining 9% of responses required more information for classification.
As presented in Table 3, negative work experiences in the domain of agreeableness primarily fell into the well-being category (44%).

text.text: Conscientiousness-related negative work experiences were mainly characterized by hindered task performance or time management (32%).
Additionally, the majority of responses concerning extraversion highlighted interpersonal difficulties at work (46%).
For openness, the largest percentage of responses fell into the task performance/time management category (38%), along with the well-being category (35%).
Lastly, 62% of respondents mentioned negative work experiences related to well-being when evaluating their perceived misfit for emotional stability.
Prevalence patterns varied greatly depending on the direction of perceived personality-work misfit (see Table 3).

text.text: For agreeableness, open responses associated with perceived deficiency (N = 31) most commonly described interpersonal difficulties (45%).
For example, one participant working as a team lead noted "(…) a somewhat distant relationship with direct employees" (item 1).
In contrast, responses preceding a perception of excess (N = 210) were predominantly linked to reports of diminished well-being (49%).
As one respondent noted: "At times, it is difficult to detach from the struggles that people at work share with me.
I have woken up at night several times as these stories weigh on my mind (…)" (item 2).
Conscientiousness.
Work experiences reported by employees perceiving deficiencies in their conscientiousness (N = 63) were mainly related to task performance and time management (57%).
One participant stated: "Not being able to find something right away leads me to postpone completing it" (item 6).
Those reporting excess conscientiousness (N = 142) detailed a more diverse range of work experiences.
The majority (36%) described interpersonal difficulties at work, for example: "People excessively turn to me because I am knowledgeable and well-prepared" (item 8).
A significant proportion (32%) mentioned wellbeing: "My systematic preparation can result in stress at the beginning of major projects.
At times, I tend to ruminate about what could go wrong (…)" (item 8).
Furthermore, 20% described work experiences related to task performance and time management: "(…) being orderly sometimes requires too much time that could have been spent on other tasks" (item 7).
Negative work experiences associated with perceived deficiency in extraversion (N = 53) were primarily linked to interpersonal difficulties at work (60%).
For example, one participant noted that this results in "Little contact with the rest of the staff.
I sometimes don't feel like I'm part of the team" (item 11).

In contrast, evaluations suggesting "too much" extraversion (N = 87) exhibited a more nuanced pattern of negative work experiences, being generally linked to both interpersonal difficulties at work (38%) and task performance and time management (32%).
An illustrative response related to interpersonal difficulties is "I tend to speak too much and repeat myself.
As a result, quieter individuals have fewer opportunities to express their opinions (…)" (item 12).

text.text: Perceived personality-work (mis)fit scores were first mean-centred within each domain, and squared terms were subsequently computed to capture potential curvilinear effects.
Three separate hierarchical regression models were estimated, one for each performance domain.
In each analysis, Model 1 included the five centred perceived (mis)fit scores, and Model 2 introduced the corresponding squared terms.
Of the six model specifications tested, five were statistically significant, although explained variance was modest (Table 4).
text.formatted: Of the six model specifications tested, five were statistically significant, although explained variance was modest (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: For task performance, the inclusion of quadratic terms in Model 2 did not significantly improve model fit (Δ adjusted R² = -.004, p = .692).

Model 1 results showed that personality-work (mis)fit in conscientiousness was positively associated with supervisor-rated task performance (β = .19, p < .001), revealing that as employees' perceived (mis)fit approached excess ("too much"), they tended to receive more favourable performance ratings.
text.formatted: Model 1 results showed that personality-work (mis)fit in conscientiousness was positively associated with supervisor-rated task performance (β = .19, p < .001), revealing that as employees' perceived (mis)fit approached excess ("too much"), they tended to receive more favourable performance ratings.

text.text: In contrast, (mis)fit in extraversion was negatively associated with task performance (β = -.11, p = .031), indicating that supervisors gave lower performance ratings as employees' perceived personality-work (mis)fit in extraversion shifted toward the "too much" end of the continuum.
For contextual performance, the addition of quadratic terms in Model 2 again did not significantly improve model fit (Δ adjusted R² = .004, p = .204).
In Model 1, perceived personality-work (mis)fit in agreeableness was positively associated with contextual performance ratings (β = .14, p = .007).
This suggests that as employees' perceived agreeableness-work (mis)fit approached excess, they received more favourable contextual performance ratings.

By contrast, (mis)fit in conscientiousness showed a negative association (β = -0.10, p = .021), indicating that when employees' perceived (mis)fit leaned toward the "too much" end of the continuum, their supervisors rated their contextual performance lower.

For adaptive performance, neither the linear model (adjusted R² = .011, p = .059) nor the addition of quadratic terms (Δ adjusted R² = .005, p = .174) yielded meaningful effects, and no individual predictors reached significance.

text.text: Much of the existing literature treats perceived fit as a broad psychological experience, often overlooking how employees evaluate the alignment of specific personal attributes-such as personality traits-with their work (Su et al., 2015).

text.text: The present study addressed this gap by introducing and empirically testing the concept of perceived personality-work (mis)fit, offering a more granular understanding of how trait-work misalignments are experienced, what shapes these perceptions, and how they relate to supervisor-rated job performance.

The TLTM scale as a tool for mapping fit, deficiency, and excess Our findings provide initial empirical support for the utility of the TLTM scale (Kaiser & Kaplan, 2005) in capturing nuanced perceived personality-work (mis)fit.

text.text: Across the Big Five domains, nearly three-quarters of employees' ratings reflected perceived misfit, with 27.6% indicating deficiency and 41.9% excess.
Importantly, this pattern reveals that misfit was not skewed toward one direction.
In fact, perceived excess was more common than deficiency for most domains, except for emotional stability, where the reverse was true.

Notably, even for openness, a domain for which the potential costs of higher scores have not yet been documented in previous work (e.g., on the TMGT effect), 42.6% of participants reported having "too much" of the trait.

This study further demonstrates that perceived personality-work (mis)fit is meaningfully associated with (Likert-rated) personality trait levels, yet offers distinct interpretive value (Research question 2).

While robust positive correlations were evident at the domain level, a more granular examination of item-level responses revealed that perceived fit ("the right amount") occurred across the personality trait spectrum, predominantly clustered around Likert scores of 3, 4, and 5.

Moreover, in instances where participants rated their personality trait as a 5 on the Likert scale, a substantial percentage (46% on average) perceived this trait level as excessive ("too much"), while 52% regarded it as appropriate.

These results suggest that perceived personality-work (mis)fit reflects more than trait magnitude-it captures perceived appropriateness in context, offering a complementary perspective to traditional trait assessments.

Our third objective was to use qualitative methods to uncover the origins of perceived personality-work (mis)fit, addressing a notable gap in broader perceived fit theory (e.g., Jansen & Shipp, 2019; Vleugels et al., 2018).

text.text: Thematic analysis revealed that negative work experiences associated with perceived personality-work (mis)fit extend well beyond in-role performance.
In fact, the most frequently mentioned category of work experiences was wellbeing (39%), followed by task performance and time management (24%), and interpersonal difficulties at work (22%).
We also identified discernible patterns across Big Five domains, as well as meaningful differences within each domain.
These within-domain variations highlight that the perceived costs associated with deficiency in a domain do not necessarily mirror those of excess.

For example, perceived deficiencies in conscientiousness were primarily linked to task performance and time management issues, whereas an excess of this trait was mainly associated with interpersonal difficulties and well-being concerns.

Finally, our findings suggest that perceived misfit can correspond to observable performance outcomes, echoing results from broader perceived fit research (e.g., Kristof-Brown et al., 2005), though the observed associations were modest and trait-specific.

text.text: Nevertheless, the fact that supervisors detected differences associated with employees' fit perceptions is noteworthy, particularly given that perceived fit is a subjective construct that only partly overlaps with objective fit (Edwards et al., 2006) and because supervisor-rated performance is substantially influenced by rater effects (Foster et al., 2024).

text.text: For example, perceived personality-work (mis)fit for conscientiousness was positively associated with task performance, indicating that perceived deficiency hindered performance, while perceived excess did not.
Conversely, for contextual performance, we observed a negative association with personality-work (mis)fit for this trait, suggesting that excess may impair performance even when deficiency does not.
These patterns align with our qualitative findings, in which participants more frequently linked conscientiousness deficiencies to task-performance problems than excesses in conscientiousness.

By examining perceived fit at the level of specific personality traits, this study extends the literature that has traditionally conceptualized perceived fit as a broad, undifferentiated experience (e.g., Su et al., 2015).

text.text: Our findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between deficiencies and excesses, as both were common and showed asymmetric relationships with performance outcomes, providing support for van Vianen's (2018) broader contention that misfit direction matters.

In addition, perceived personality-work (mis)fit showed only partial overlap with personality trait levels, suggesting that these perceptions represent subjective evaluations of trait-environment alignment rather than mere reflections of personality trait levels alone.

Qualitative findings further showed that these evaluations are informed by diverse workplace experiences, including well-being, task performance, and interpersonal functioning, consistent with recent calls to give greater attention to well-being outcomes in work psychology (Tay et al., 2023).

text.text: Methodologically, the study introduces a novel operationalization of perceived personality-work (mis)fit using the TLTM scale (Kaiser & Kaplan, 2005), which may serve as a template for assessing perceived fit in relation to other personal attributes (e.g., skills or values).

text.text: Although psychometric results were generally acceptable, weaker reliability and structural validity emerged for openness and, to a lesser extent, conscientiousness.

This may reflect the evaluative nature of perceived fit judgments, whereby items within the same trait domain can vary in their relevance to specific work-related demands and outcomes (e.g., Stewart et al., 2021).

text.text: Practically, our findings offer actionable insights for organizations and career counsellors seeking to improve personality-work fit.

Misfit experiences may serve as selfregulatory signals that motivate individuals to restore fit by changing either their work environment (i.e., job crafting) or their own personality traits (i.e., volitional personality change) (Dupré & Wille, 2025; Kandler et al., 2024).

text.text: By identifying which traits are perceived as misaligned, in what direction, and why, the present approach can help guide more targeted interventions.
A number of study limitations need to be recognized.

First, while our choice of the ORG-B5 instrument was guided by its recognition as one of the few validated and concise contextualized personality measures, it did not include other relevant domains such as honesty-humility (Johnson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: First, while our choice of the ORG-B5 instrument was guided by its recognition as one of the few validated and concise contextualized personality measures, it did not include other relevant domains such as honesty-humility <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Johnson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the instrument's brevity has implications for domain coverage.
For instance, within conscientiousness, two of the four ORG-B5 items focus on orderliness, while other potentially meaningful facets-such as perfectionismremain unrepresented (Ashton & Lee, 2007).
text.formatted: For instance, within conscientiousness, two of the four ORG-B5 items focus on orderliness, while other potentially meaningful facets-such as perfectionismremain unrepresented <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ashton & Lee, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Another limitation is that our survey-based qualitative approach yielded a substantial proportion of irrelevant responses: 30% did not mention any negative work experiences.
While an interview-based methodology could offer greater depth and allow for follow-up questions, it would inevitably yield far less data.
Although only 21% of open-ended questions received a response, our large sample size enabled a substantial volume of open responses (N = 1225), representing 83% of participants.

This broad coverage is crucial, as it helps ensure diverse representation and addresses concerns from prior research (Miller & Lambert, 2014) about potential bias arising from group differences in non-responders.

text.text: Lastly, while our measurement approach allowed differentiation between the two directions of personality-work misfit (i.e., excess versus deficiency), it did not distinguish between different types of fit.

Specifically, it did not capture whether fit arises when both personality and work demands are high, or both are low-configurations that have been shown to yield distinct outcomes in broader fit research (van Vianen, 2018).
We discuss three future research questions that warrant further exploration.

First, the recent call for more organizational research using well-being as a criterion (Tay et al., 2023), along with insights from our qualitative data, provide a compelling case for extending our investigation into the predictive validity of perceived personality-work (mis)fit to other work outcomes.
text.formatted: First, the recent call for more organizational research using well-being as a criterion <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tay et al., 2023)</ref>, along with insights from our qualitative data, provide a compelling case for extending our investigation into the predictive validity of perceived personality-work (mis)fit to other work outcomes.

text.text: Second, while our approach examined personality domains in isolation-a strength in terms of conceptual clarity-it may have overlooked meaningful interactions between traits.
It is plausible that perceived personality-work (mis)fit for one domain depends on the level of another.

For instance, participants who reported an excess of conscientiousness may have done so in light of a combination of high conscientiousness and high neuroticism, which could contribute to a perfectionistic tendency linked to maladaptive outcomes (Smith et al., 2019).

text.text: Finally, questions of causality remain open: do negative work experiences give rise to perceived misfit, or does perceived misfit itself contribute to adverse experiences?
It is likely that these processes unfold through dynamic feedback loops over time.

Longitudinal research is needed to capture the temporal dynamics through which perceived personality-work misfit is construed in interaction with the work environment (see, e.g., Vleugels et al., 2018).

text.text: This article introduced perceived personality-work (mis)fit as a more attribute-specific approach to understanding perceived fit.

To this end, a new measurement approach was presented in which existing personality trait items are rated using a TLTM format, which allows the mapping of both perceived excess and perceived deficiency.
Through the analysis of extensive qualitative data, we also provided initial insights into the negative work experiences associated with perceptions of personality-work misfit.
Finally, our multiinformant design showed that some of these (self-) perceptions were also reflected in supervisor ratings of job performance.

We propose the following research questions: Research Question 1 (RQ1): To what extent do employees report perceived personality-work fit, deficiency, or excess, and how do these perceptions vary across the Big Five domains?

In contrast, those perceiving their level of emotional stability as excessive mentioned a broader range of work experiences (N = 21), with the three most frequently mentioned categories being interpersonal difficulties at work (33%), well-being (29%), and reputation at work (19%).
